Period schedule:
  Row 1: 40 minutes × 4 periods = 160 minutes
Total: 4 periods · 2h 40min

periods.activity_title: Picture Walk: Entering the Busy Street Scene

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Picture reading (pp.102–103): observe shops, dustbins, animals, and street figures.

time_bands.activity: Teacher walks students through the street scene on pp.102–103 picture by picture — left side shops (Vastra Style, grocery), right side (Good Meals stall, fruit vendor), bullock cart, bicycle, and the rainbow and kite above. Students are invited to name what they see before any question is posed.

Picture reading (pp.102–103): Teacher draws attention to the two dustbins (blue and green) near the food stall and the man in dark glasses with a white cane, asking students what they notice. Pairs share observations aloud before the teacher extends understanding of waste segregation and the white cane as a mobility aid.

Picture reading (pp.102–103): Focus shifts to the animals — goat herd, cat on rooftop, the dog on a leash, and birds in the sky. Students count the bullock carts and name every animal they can find, with the teacher pointing to each in turn.
Quick whole-class share: students take turns naming one thing on each side of the street, building a collective verbal inventory of the scene to consolidate observation.

periods.teacher_notes: The picture carries several layers of meaning — occupational diversity, environmental awareness through colour-coded dustbins, and social inclusion through the man with a white cane — so pace the walk to let each layer land before moving on. Students often overlook the cat on the rooftop and the kite in the sky; direct pointing helps. Where a student names something in their home language first, accept it warmly and supply the English word alongside.

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Picture reading (pp.102–103): discuss dustbins, white cane, golas, and animals in detail.

time_bands.activity: Students look at the street scene on pp.102–103 again. Teacher invites two or three students to describe what they remember from the scene in their own words, then settles the class on the picture before questions begin.

Picture reading (pp.102–103): Teacher poses the dustbin question — why two bins, why blue and green — as a class discussion. Students share what they know; teacher guides them to the idea of waste segregation (wet/dry or recyclable/non-recyclable waste), using the picture as the anchor.

Picture reading (pp.102–103): Teacher asks why the man in dark glasses carries a white stick and who the children with ice golas are, drawing out both the concept of visual impairment as a lived reality and the name 'gola' for the coloured ice treat. Students respond in short spoken sentences.

Students name all the animals they can find on pp.102–103 — goats, dog, cat, birds — while the teacher lists them on the board. The session closes with students saying one sentence each about an animal of their choice from the picture.

periods.teacher_notes: Having explored the shops, cart, and sky in the picture walk, this discussion drills deeper into the human and animal elements. The white cane and dark glasses together signal visual impairment — if students confuse 'sunglasses for fashion' with 'cane for navigation', hold the conversation gently and let the picture's evidence guide them. The gola is a culturally familiar treat for many students; connecting it to personal experience before naming it in English bridges home knowledge to the text.

periods.activity_title: Talking About the Street: Free and Guided Conversation

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Picture reading (pp.102–103): guided oral discussion linking street scene to personal experience.

time_bands.activity: Teacher opens by asking students if they have ever walked down a busy market street — a fruit stall, a clothing shop, animals crossing the road. Students share one memory each in a brief free conversation before attention returns to pp.102–103.

Picture reading (pp.102–103): guided conversation in pairs — one student describes what the woman in the green sari is doing while the other listens and adds a detail, then partners swap. Teacher circulates, prompting with 'What else do you see near her?' or 'Why do you think the goats are crossing right now?'

Whole-class guided conversation: Teacher invites students to notice the sky in the picture on pp.102–103 — the kite, the rainbow, the coloured birds — and asks what they think the weather is like and how the street might feel. Students respond in complete spoken sentences, building descriptive oral language.

Each student says one sentence aloud that begins 'In this street I can see…', choosing a detail not yet mentioned by another student. Teacher acknowledges each contribution and closes the conversation by naming the richness of the community the picture shows.

periods.teacher_notes: Having discussed the scene's details closely, students now practise sustained speaking rather than single-word answers. The pairing activity is intentionally unhurried — wait for students to produce a full sentence before moving on, even if a prompt is needed. The sky observation in the third band connects the title of the chapter to the picture directly; guiding students to notice rainbow and birds above the street enriches both vocabulary and a sense of the scene's completeness.

periods.activity_title: Whole-Chapter Synthesis: The Street Scene Revisited

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Picture reading (pp.102–103): summarise shops, people, sky, and animals across the scene.
Picture reading (pp.102–103): retell the street scene as a spoken narrative to the class.

time_bands.activity: Students open pp.102–103 and scan the whole scene silently for a brief, unhurried look. Teacher then asks: 'If you had to tell someone who has never seen this picture what is happening on this street, where would you start?' — inviting students to think about sequence and selection before speaking.

Picture reading (pp.102–103): teacher-led summarising — class builds a spoken summary together, moving from left to right across the street: shops and their names, the people and vehicles, the animals, the children with golas, and finally the sky with its kite, rainbow, and birds. Teacher scribes key ideas on the board in short phrases.

Oracy — retelling: individual students take turns retelling the street scene in two or three sentences to the class, using the board phrases as a scaffold but not reading them word for word. Teacher encourages vivid choices: 'Can you say something about the colour?' or 'What is the man with the white cane doing?'

Closing reflection: teacher asks the class what makes this street a community — drawing together the ideas of different occupations (vendor, fruit seller, restaurant), inclusion (man with white cane), environmental care (two dustbins), and the natural world above (sky, birds, rainbow, kite). Students give one-word or one-phrase answers to close.

periods.teacher_notes: This synthesis draws on everything the picture has offered — observation, vocabulary, personal connection, and community themes. Students who engage with the summarising board phrases will find the retelling more accessible; those who are confident speakers can be invited to go beyond the board. The closing reflection on community is not a new concept but a naming of what the picture has always shown — occupation, inclusion, environment, and sky together.
materials: Blackboard or whiteboard for scribing summary phrases

items.item_stem: Look at the street scene on Textbook pages 102–103. Two dustbins stand near the food stall — one is blue and one is green. Why are there two different-coloured dustbins?

options.label: A
options.text: Blue bins are kept outside shops and green bins are kept near roads.

options.label: B
options.text: One bin is for wet waste and the other is for dry or recyclable waste.

options.label: C
options.text: The blue bin is for the food stall and the green bin is for the fruit vendor.

options.label: D
options.text: They are painted different colours so children can tell them apart from far away.

what_each_option_reveals.C: Student sees the dustbins as belonging to nearby stalls rather than as a shared waste-segregation system.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Student focuses on visibility as a practical reason rather than on the environmental purpose of colour coding.
what_each_option_reveals.A: Student infers a location-based rule that the picture does not support, missing the concept of waste segregation.

items.source_lo: Student observes and interprets a detailed community scene using a picture narrative as the vehicle.

items.item_stem: Look at the street scene on Textbook pages 102–103. A man in dark glasses is walking with a white cane. What does the white cane tell us about this person, and what does it help him do?

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: The white cane tells us the man cannot see well — he is visually impaired. The cane helps him feel the path in front of him so he can walk safely without bumping into things.

items.item_stem: Look at the street scene on Textbook pages 102–103. Which of the following best describes what is happening on the street?

options.label: A
options.text: A busy street with shops, people, animals, and children going about daily life.

options.label: B
options.text: A school street where children are playing games outside their classroom.

options.label: C
options.text: It is a quiet road with only a few animals walking past.

options.label: D
options.text: People are gathered for a festival and all the shops are closed.

what_each_option_reveals.D: Student associates a crowded, colourful scene with a festival rather than reading the details of open shops and daily activity.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Student focuses only on the animals visible in the scene and misses the full range of human activity.
what_each_option_reveals.B: Student draws on a familiar school-setting schema instead of reading the picture's clues about a market street.

items.item_stem: Look at the street scene on Textbook pages 102–103. In two or three sentences, describe to your partner what is happening on this street. Tell them about the people, the animals, and what you can see in the sky.

expected_elements: Names at least two people or activities on the street.
Mentions at least one animal from the scene.
Says something about the sky, kite, rainbow, or birds.
